summary: This RFC compares several data representation standards: CCITT X.409, the NBS Computer Based Message System standard, DARPA Multimedia Mail, Courier, and Sun RPC. It proposes no standard for the ARPA Internet.

plainLanguage.summary: Different computers write numbers and words in different ways. This note lines up several ways to do it and compares them.

questions: compare x.409 courier and sun rpc
what is implicit versus explicit representation
subtitle: Comparing five approaches to encoding data in networked systems.

tldr.problem: Different computer systems need to exchange data, but they represent numbers and text differently. This survey compares five standards for encoding data to be sent over networks.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC examines how CCITT X.409, NBS Computer Based Message System, DARPA Multimedia Mail, XEROX Courier, and SUN Remote Procedure Call each define data types and encode them for transmission.
tldr.outcome: The CCITT X.409 standard has gained wide acceptance internationally and can represent most of the data elements defined in the other standards, making it a good choice for systems that include many different kinds of computers.

today: This RFC is an informational survey with no standards proposal. It remains a useful historical comparison of how different communities approached the problem of representing data in networked systems.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 971 compares several data representation standards being used to encode data for transmission across networks. The RFC examines CCITT X.409 (an international standard for message handling), the NBS Computer Based Message System (a U.S. federal standard), DARPA Multimedia Mail (an experimental system), XEROX Courier (a remote procedure call protocol), and the SUN Remote Procedure Call package (which implements network communication between UNIX machines).

The goal is to compare these standards and understand how the CCITT standard, which is gaining worldwide acceptance, compares with other standards developed for electronic mail, distributed computing, and remote procedure calls.
sections.plainLanguage: There are five different ways that computers use to write down data for sending over networks. The memo looks at each one to see how they work.

sections.title: Two Categories of Standards
sections.content:
The standards fall into two categories based on their intended use. Interprocess communication standards like Courier and SUN RPC are designed for communication between similar machines running the same programming language. These standards define data types that map directly to programming language types, making conversion quick and efficient when both computers are the same type.

Message standards like X.409, NBS CBMS, and DARPA Multimedia Mail are designed for communication between many different kinds of computers and programming languages. These standards define more general and flexible type systems because they must work across diverse environments.
sections.plainLanguage: Some standards are for talking between similar computers that understand the same programming language. Others are for sending messages between completely different computers that might not have much in common.

sections.title: Implicit Versus Explicit Representation
sections.content:
The RFC identifies a key difference in how these standards handle type information. Implicit representation, used by Courier and SUN RPC, means the sender and receiver must agree in advance on the structure and types of the data being sent. The data itself contains only values, not type information. This reduces the message size but requires both parties to know the format beforehand.

Explicit representation, used by X.409, NBS CBMS, and DARPA Multimedia Mail, includes type and length information in the message itself. This makes messages larger but allows a receiver to handle data types it has never seen before, and it provides flexibility for future expansion and optional fields.
sections.plainLanguage: One way is to agree ahead of time what the numbers mean, and just send the numbers. Another way is to send the numbers with labels that say what they mean, so the receiver can figure it out even if it's different from what it expected.

sections.title: Comparison of Data Types
sections.content: The RFC provides a detailed comparison table of the data types supported by each standard. All five standards support basic types like integers and strings, but they differ in coverage. CCITT X.409 is the most comprehensive, offering types for booleans, various sizes of integers, bit strings, multiple character encodings, dates, and times. SUN RPC includes floating-point numbers, which CCITT X.409 lacks. Courier includes procedure types. DARPA Multimedia Mail and NBS CBMS include support for encryption and compression. The standards also differ in how they represent structured data like sequences and records.
sections.plainLanguage: Each standard has a list of types it can send, like numbers, words, lists of things, and dates. Some standards have more types than others, and some have types that the others don't have.

sections.title: Conclusions
sections.content:
The RFC concludes that CCITT X.409 is the clear leader in international adoption. For Internet applications that include many different kinds of computers, a standard using explicit representation like X.409 is preferable because it allows computers to communicate even when they have not been configured in advance to understand each other. The RFC notes that X.409 can construct most data elements from the other standards, though it lacks floating-point numbers.

However, the RFC warns that some flexibility in X.409, such as the private-use class that allows custom extensions, could lead to confusion and lack of coordination between different implementations. If X.409 were adopted for the ARPANET, a carefully defined subset would probably need to be selected to ensure interoperability.
sections.plainLanguage: X.409 is winning worldwide. For computers on the Internet that don't know each other, X.409 works best because it includes descriptions of what the data means. But if you use it, you have to agree on which of its features you are going to use.
